recipe.history:
Chili in the American culinary tradition is a dish with deep and contested roots, but its Southwestern and Tex-Mex origins are indisputable. The earliest documented versions — what food historians call chili con carne — emerged in San Antonio, Texas, in the nineteenth century, sold by the famous Chili Queens in the city's plazas and markets. These women, many of them of Mexican and indigenous descent, ladled fiery beef and chili pepper stews from iron cauldrons over open fires, and their product became famous enough to attract visitors from across the country. Traditional Texas chili con carne is a purist's preparation: beef, dried chilies, cumin, and garlic, with no beans and no tomatoes by strict Texas convention — a dish as austere and intense as the landscape that produced it. Philadelphia's relationship with chili is more recent and more eclectic: the city's diverse immigrant communities and its tradition of hearty working-class food created space for chili variations that diverged sharply from the Texan original. White bean chili with chicken and poblanos — a Southwestern-influenced preparation popularized in the 1980s and 1990s — represents a distinctly non-traditional line of chili evolution, building on the structure of the original but substituting white beans for red, chicken for beef, and green chilies for dried red ones, resulting in something simultaneously familiar and entirely different.

Chili on burgers has a long and glorious history in American diner culture, from the simple chili cheeseburger of the Midwest to the elaborate chili burger constructions of California drive-ins. The chili burger at Tommy's in Los Angeles — a soupy, aggressive beef chili ladled over a double patty since 1946 — is arguably the most famous, but across America every regional chili tradition has at some point been applied to a burger. The white chicken chili variation brings a different set of flavors to a beef patty: the creamy, mild heat of poblano cream, the earthiness of white beans, and the tang of white cheddar create a topping that complements rather than overwhelms the beef. The pretzel bun, a German-American contribution to the burger bun tradition, adds its distinctive lye-induced browning, chewy crumb, and slight bitterness — a structural and flavor element that can stand up to the density of a chili topping in ways that a standard brioche cannot.

I made a white chicken chili for the first time during a cold snap in February, cooking it in a large pot on the back burner while the rest of the kitchen was used for other things. By the time it was done, the whole apartment smelled like toasted cumin and charred poblano and warm cream, and I stood at the stove eating it directly from the pot with a piece of bread because I could not wait for a bowl. I still have not found a way to improve on the basic formula — white beans softened in chicken broth, poblanos charred and peeled, a long simmer until everything collapses into a silky, fragrant stew. Putting that stew on a burger felt like an obvious progression, and the pretzel bun revealed itself as the perfect vehicle the first time I tried it: its chew and its slight saltiness made the whole thing feel complete in a way I had not anticipated.

The white chicken chili and poblano cream in this burger are rich, creamy, and substantial. They demand a patty that is equally substantial — and medium rare at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit is the only temperature that produces a patty worthy of those toppings. The fat that remains in the meat at medium rare is the fat that lubricates every bite and carries flavor throughout the burger. Cook the patty further and you drive out that fat, creating a dry, fibrous puck that sinks under the weight of the chili topping without contributing anything of its own. Medium rare is where beef meets its toppings as an equal, not as a substrate.
ingredients: For the white bean chicken chili:
2 poblano peppers, roasted, peeled, seeded, and diced
1 can (15 oz) white beans (cannellini or Great Northern), drained
1 can (15 oz) white beans, kept whole for texture
1 poblano pepper, roasted, peeled, and seeded
instructions: 1. Roast the poblanos: Place poblano peppers directly over a gas flame or under a broiler, turning with tongs until charred on all sides. Transfer to a bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and let steam 15 minutes. Peel off charred skin, discard seeds, and dice the flesh. Reserve two roasted poblanos for the chili and one for the poblano cream.

2. Make the white bean chicken chili: Heat olive oil in a medium saucepan over medium-high heat. Season chicken thighs with salt and pepper and sear 4 minutes per side until golden. Remove and set aside. In the same pan, sauté onion until softened, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and cook 1 minute. Add diced roasted poblano, cumin, coriander, oregano, and cayenne; cook 1 minute until fragrant.

3. Add both cans of beans and chicken broth. Shred or dice the seared chicken and return it to the pot. Bring to a simmer and cook 25 to 30 minutes until the chili thickens. Mash about one-third of the beans against the side of the pot to naturally thicken the broth. Add lime juice, season with salt and pepper. Keep warm.
4. Make the poblano cream: Combine roasted poblano, sour cream, cream cheese, garlic, and lime juice in a blender. Blend until completely smooth. Season with salt. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Make the pretzel buns: Combine warm water and yeast with sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let sit 5 minutes. Add salt and softened butter. Add flour one cup at a time using the dough hook on low. Increase speed to medium and knead 7 to 8 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and rise at room temperature 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
6. Divide dough into 4 equal portions. Shape each into a tight ball. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover loosely and proof 30 to 45 minutes.

7. Preheat oven to 425°F. Bring 8 cups water and baking soda to a boil in a wide saucepan. Using a slotted spoon, gently lower each bun into the baking soda bath for 30 seconds, flipping once. Return to parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush with egg wash, score the top with a sharp knife in a cross pattern, and sprinkle with pretzel salt. Bake 15 to 18 minutes until deep mahogany brown. Cool briefly before slicing.

8. Form the patties: Gently mix cumin into the ground beef. Divide into 4 portions and form into 4-inch patties, 3/4-inch thick, with a dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Refrigerate 15 minutes.

9. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat, lightly oil the surface. Sear patties dimple-side up for 3 minutes undisturbed. Flip once, place a slice of white cheddar on each, and cook 2 to 3 more minutes until internal temperature reaches 130 to 135°F. Remove from heat, tent with foil, and rest 3 minutes.
10. Split pretzel buns and toast cut-side down in butter over medium heat in the skillet until warmed and lightly crisped, about 60 to 90 seconds.

11. Assemble the burgers: Spread poblano cream generously on both cut sides of the pretzel bun. Place the rested patty with melted white cheddar on the bottom bun. Ladle a generous portion of white bean chicken chili over the patty and cheese. Add a few pickled jalapeño slices. Scatter fresh cilantro leaves over the top. Close with the top bun. Serve immediately with additional chili on the side.
